title: Origin, Corporate Evolution & Past Business Cycles
book_title: From a Somerset Public Library to the Cloud Control Plane

epigraph.quote: Every platform shift creates two fortunes: one for the company that builds the highway, and another for the company that builds the guardrails, tollbooths, and tow trucks.
epigraph.author: Enterprise Infrastructure Maxim

web_blocks.html: Dr. Tianyi "TJ" Jiang and Xunkai "Kai" Gong founded AvePoint, Inc. in July 2001 in Somerset, New Jersey [18, 19]. They wrote their early enterprise infrastructure code out of a public library during the dot-com downturn [18, 19]. Most startups of that era chased consumer internet traffic. Jiang and Gong instead targeted an unglamorous enterprise bottleneck inside Microsoft SharePoint. As large corporations adopted SharePoint for document collaboration, native admin tools fell short. IT teams lacked granular backup, item-level recovery, content migration, and permissions auditing. AvePoint's flagship on-premises suite, DocAve, solved those exact operational failures. That focus let the company compound profitably for nearly two decades before tapping public equity markets [19].

Between 2001 and 2020, AvePoint survived three technology and capital cycles without losing founder control [19]. Kai Gong served as CEO until 2009, when he and TJ Jiang became Co-CEOs. In 2020, Jiang became sole CEO while Gong moved to Executive Chairman [19]. Both co-founders still hold those roles today. Along the way, AvePoint took minority growth capital from Summit Partners, Goldman Sachs, and TPG Sixth Street Partners. That capital funded expansion across North America, EMEA, and APAC. It also anchored Singapore as AvePoint's Asia headquarters and a major international R&D hub [13, 19]. When Microsoft shifted from on-premises SharePoint to Office 365, AvePoint rebuilt DocAve for multi-tenant cloud APIs early enough to capture the enterprise migration wave [19]. That early cloud rewrite turned a legacy SharePoint toolmaker into a global SaaS platform [19].

web_blocks.takeaway: Unlike zero-interest-rate SaaS startups born in 2019, AvePoint spent 20 years solving Microsoft ecosystem data-management complexity before going public, then pivoted rapidly from post-SPAC operating losses to GAAP profitability by FY2024.

web_blocks.html: The company's hardest strategic test arrived with its 2021 public debut and the 2022–2023 software downturn. On July 1, 2021, AvePoint closed its merger with Apex Technology Acquisition Corporation (APXT), a SPAC led by Jeff Epstein and Brad Koenig [18]. Shares began trading on Nasdaq on July 2, 2021 [18]. Like most 2021 SPAC peers, AvePoint absorbed heavy stock-based compensation ($59.5M in FY2021) and a $(53.5)M GAAP operating loss [1, 6]. At the same time, management actively cannibalized high-margin perpetual licenses and maintenance to move customers onto multi-year SaaS subscriptions [1, 6]. That deliberate mix shift depressed headline revenue optics in 2022–2023 while building a far stickier recurring base [2, 6].

Many SPAC-era software vendors stalled when capital tightened in 2022. AvePoint instead executed a disciplined two-year operational reset. Management kept operating expense growth well below SaaS revenue growth. It also expanded channel and Managed Service Provider (MSP) distribution to lower customer acquisition costs. Enterprise AI readiness—specifically Microsoft 365 Copilot oversharing and data hygiene—became the next growth catalyst [2, 7]. By FY2024, AvePoint crossed into GAAP operating profitability ($7.2M). In FY2025, it delivered $33.0M in GAAP operating income and $35.1M in GAAP net income. On September 19, 2025, AvePoint also completed a secondary listing on the Singapore Exchange (SGX: AVP) [2, 13]. By Q3 2026, Annual Recurring Revenue reached $495.1M (+27% YoY), proving that the 2022–2024 reset built a durable growth engine [3].

web_blocks.mechanism: A SaaS backup vendor that attempted to escape low-margin SMB backup commoditization through debt-funded M&A (acquiring EVault in 2015 and Webroot in 2019), stretching integration capacity and compressing operating margins.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: Stagnant organic growth and integration debt forced a rescue sale to OpenText in late 2019 for $1.42 billion ($23 per share), well below historical SaaS growth expectations.
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: In data protection, bolt-on M&A without unified platform architecture destroys margins. AvePoint's tuck-in deals (tyGraph, Ydentic) have been small, cash-funded, and integrated directly into the Confidence Platform—a discipline investors must verify continues.

web_blocks.title: Why the 2021–2024 Model Transition Matters
paragraphs: In FY2021, SaaS accounted for just 44.6% of AvePoint's $191.9M revenue ($85.6M) [6]. Term License, Maintenance, Services, and Perpetual Licenses made up the other 55.4% [6]. By FY2025, SaaS reached $319.2M, or 76.1% of total revenue [2]. In Q3 2026, SaaS hit $105.5M, or 80.5% of quarterly revenue [3]. That mix shift hid top-line resilience during 2022–2023. Today, it drives gross margin expansion and durable recurring cash flow.

The September 2025 Singapore Exchange (SGX: AVP) secondary listing also carries clear commercial weight [13]. AvePoint runs its Asia headquarters and major R&D operations out of Singapore [13]. Dual-listing alongside Nasdaq anchors the brand with Asian sovereign, banking, and public-sector buyers. It also gives APAC institutional investors direct equity access without changing US governance [13]. Across twenty-five years, founder-led engineering discipline has kept AvePoint focused on durable cash flow over debt-funded roll-ups [19].

book_paragraphs: To understand AvePoint properly, you and I have to resist the temptation to lump it in with the speculative software cohort that went public via SPAC in 2021. Yes, AvePoint used a SPAC vehicle—Apex Technology Acquisition Corporation—to list on Nasdaq in July 2021. On the surface, that single fact explains why many institutional investors initially treated it with skepticism. Yet underneath the listing mechanics sat a twenty-year-old enterprise software business that started in a Somerset, New Jersey public library in 2001.

Dr. Tianyi 'TJ' Jiang and Kai Gong did not set out to build a consumer app or chase venture-subsidized blitzscaling. In the aftermath of the dot-com bust, they found a real, recurring engineering headache inside Fortune 500 IT departments: Microsoft SharePoint was spreading rapidly across enterprises, and Microsoft's native administrative tools could not cleanly migrate, back up, or govern the sprawling permissions trees that resulted. Their first product, DocAve, became the Swiss Army knife for SharePoint administrators.

book_subsections.title: Bootstrapping Through Two Platform Shifts (2001–2019)
paragraphs: Think about how rare it is for an enterprise software company to survive twenty-five years with both co-founders still at the helm. Kai Gong served as CEO until 2009, when he and TJ Jiang shared the Co-CEO title; in 2020, Jiang stepped into the sole CEO seat while Gong transitioned to Executive Chairman. Unlike venture-backed startups that burn through three chief executives before finding product-market fit, AvePoint compounded organically out of New Jersey for years before taking minority growth investments from Summit Partners, Goldman Sachs, and TPG Sixth Street Partners.

That capital was not used to subsidize money-losing domestic marketing. Instead, AvePoint used it to build an international R&D and commercial footprint across North America, EMEA, and Asia-Pacific—establishing Singapore as its Asian headquarters and engineering hub. When Microsoft pivoted from on-premises SharePoint servers to cloud-hosted Office 365 and Microsoft 365 in the 2010s, AvePoint had to rebuild its entire product architecture for multi-tenant cloud APIs. Many legacy SharePoint vendors died in that crossing. AvePoint survived because it re-engineered DocAve into cloud-native SaaS early enough to ride the enterprise migration wave.

book_subsections.title: The SPAC Overhang and the 2022–2024 Operational Reset
paragraphs: When AvePoint merged with Apex Technology Acquisition Corporation on July 1, 2021, it walked straight into two simultaneous storms. The first was external: the 2022–2023 software bear market, which punished any company with GAAP operating losses and heavy stock-based compensation. In FY2021, AvePoint posted $191.9 million in revenue, a $(53.5) million GAAP operating loss, and $59.5 million in stock-based compensation. To a casual screener, it looked like every other bloated SPAC.

The second storm was internal and deliberate: AvePoint was actively cannibalizing its own legacy business. In FY2021, SaaS represented just 44.6% of revenue ($85.6 million), while term licenses, maintenance, services, and perpetual licenses made up the remaining 55.4%. Over the next four years, management pushed customers off perpetual and maintenance contracts and into multi-year SaaS subscriptions. That transition suppressed headline revenue growth optically during 2022 and 2023, even as underlying SaaS revenue compounded above 35% annually.

What separates AvePoint from the Carbonites of the world—companies that tried to buy growth with debt-bloated M&A and ended up in rescue sales—is how TJ Jiang responded when capital tightened. Rather than defending top-line optics with undisciplined sales burn, AvePoint froze low-ROI overhead, leaned into channel partners and Managed Service Providers, and kept acquisitions small, cash-funded, and architectural, such as tyGraph in 2022 and Ydentic in 2025.

book_subsections.title: The AI Governance Wave and the 2025–2026 Inflection
paragraphs: By FY2024, the reset paid off: revenue reached $330.5 million, SaaS hit 69.8% of the mix, and GAAP operating income turned positive at $7.2 million. In FY2025, revenue accelerated 27% to $419.5 million, GAAP operating income quadrupled to $33.0 million, GAAP net income reached $35.1 million, and AvePoint completed a secondary listing on the Singapore Exchange (SGX: AVP) in September 2025—becoming the first B2B SaaS company dual-listed on both Nasdaq and SGX. By Q3 2026, Annual Recurring Revenue reached $495.1 million, propelled by enterprises scrambling to lock down data permissions before rolling out Microsoft 365 Copilot and autonomous AI agents.

Pause for a moment and appreciate the strategic logic of that Singapore secondary listing. Most US-listed mid-cap software companies treat Asia-Pacific as a minor sales outpost run out of a regional distributor. AvePoint instead has nearly 29% of its GAAP revenue in APAC ($95.4 million in FY2024) and runs its international R&D hub out of Singapore. By listing on SGX alongside Nasdaq, management anchored its brand with Asian sovereign, banking, and public-sector buyers who value local governance and regulatory alignment, while giving regional institutional investors direct access to the equity.

When you step back and view the entire 2001–2026 arc, a clear pattern emerges. AvePoint has never been a momentum story built on one hot product cycle. It survived the post-dot-com slump by solving SharePoint farm administration; it survived the cloud transition by rewriting DocAve into multi-tenant SaaS; it survived the 2022–2023 SaaS bear market by cutting burn and scaling its partner channel; and it is now riding the enterprise AI governance wave with a profitable, self-funding balance sheet. That kind of multi-cycle durability is rare in mid-cap software.

book_subsections.title: What the Carbonite Failure Base Rate Teaches Us
paragraphs: Whenever a data-protection vendor grows into the $400 million to $500 million revenue band, investors should study the graveyard of peers that stumbled at the same scale. Carbonite is the cleanest cautionary parallel. After going public in 2011, Carbonite tried to outrun low-margin consumer and SMB backup commoditization by executing debt-funded acquisitions—buying EVault in 2015 and Webroot in 2019. Instead of creating a unified platform, the acquisitions bloated debt, fractured engineering focus, and compressed margins until OpenText bought Carbonite in late 2019 for $1.42 billion, or $23 per share.

AvePoint has thus far avoided every trap in that playbook. Its acquisitions—tyGraph in 2022 and Ydentic in 2025—were small, cash-funded, and snapped directly into the Confidence Platform rather than bolted on as separate billing stacks. Keeping that architectural discipline intact as ARR marches toward $1 billion is the single most important governance test for TJ Jiang and Kai Gong.

Think about what this means for how you and I underwrite the company's culture. In enterprise software, founder-led businesses that survived two decades of technological disruption without serial equity dilution or debt-fueled roll-ups tend to share a specific trait: engineering pragmatism over financial engineering. AvePoint did not invent a buzzword first and hunt for customers later; it solved SharePoint backup in 2001, rebuilt for Microsoft 365 cloud governance in the 2010s, endured the painful SPAC-era accounting transition in 2021–2023, and emerged in 2025–2026 with GAAP profitability and nearly $500 million in recurring revenue.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Twenty-five years of surviving Microsoft platform transitions—from on-premises SharePoint to Microsoft 365 to Copilot—is not luck. It is institutional muscle memory. The question for us in the chapters ahead is whether that muscle memory translates into durable, high-ROIC compounding or gets squeezed as Microsoft itself moves up the data-governance stack.
